tip: -(으)ㄹ게요 = I'll (a promise to the listener): 카톡할게요 (katokalgeyo).
쓰다 (sseuda) means both 'use' and 'write': 이모티콘을 써요 (imotikoneul sseoyo) = I use stickers. The same verb also writes letters and texts.
좀 (jom) softens requests: 좀 알려 주세요 (jom allyeo juseyo) = please let me know.
-아/어 놓다 (-a/eo nota) marks a state you set and leave in place: 무음으로 해 놓아요 (mueumeuro hae noayo) = set it to silent and keep it that way.
다 (da) before a verb means completely: 데이터를 다 썼어요 (deitareul da sseosseoyo) = used up all the data. Works with other verbs too – 다 먹었어요 (da meogeosseoyo) = ate it all.
다 됐어요 (da dwaesseoyo), literally 'has all become', is the everyday 'it died / ran out': 배터리가 다 됐어요 (baeteoriga da dwaesseoyo). Works for parking time too.
V-어 주세요 = please (do for me): 빌려 주세요 (billyeo juseyo) = please lend me.
English 'left it at home' is two verbs in Korean: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = put it down and came. You say both the placing – 놓다 (nota) – and the coming – 오다 (oda).
-고 있어요 = is ...ing: 충전하고 있어요 (chungjeonhago isseoyo) = is charging.
-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 = can: 충전할 수 있어요? (chungjeonhal su isseoyo?) = can I charge?
V-어 보세요 = try ...ing: 써 보세요 (sseo boseyo) = try it out.
못 (mot) = can't, blocked or unable – different from 안 (an) = simply don't: 로그인을 못 했어요 (rogeineul mot haesseoyo) means the login failed, not that you skipped it.
찍을까요? (jjigeulkkayo?) – the -(으)ㄹ까요 ending means 'shall we?'. Korean has no separate word for 'shall'; the whole suggestion lives in the verb ending.
꺼지다 (kkeojida) = turn off by itself; 끄다 (kkeuda) = turn it off. 갑자기 꺼졌어요 (gapjagi kkeojyeosseoyo) blames the phone – nobody switched it off.
Sound comes out on its own in Korean – 소리가 나다 (soriga nada = sound emerges). So 'no sound' is 소리가 안 나요 (soriga an nayo): the sound isn't coming out.
-비 (-bi) tacks 'fee' onto almost anything: 수리비가 (suribiga) = the repair cost, 택시비 (taeksibi) = taxi fare, 교통비 (gyotongbi) = transport costs.
-게 (-ge) turns an adjective into a how-word: 길다 (gilda = long) becomes 길게 눌러 주세요 (gilge nulleo juseyo) = press long, i.e. long-press.
-(으)면 돼요 = just do X: 누르면 돼요 (nureumyeon dwaeyo) = pressing works.
V-ㄴ + noun = that I ...ed: 주문한 옷 (jumunhan ot) = the clothes I ordered.
-아서 = so: 안 맞아서 환불했어요 (an majaseo hwanbulhaesseoyo).
때 (ttae) after a noun means 'at the time of': 세일 때 (seil ttae) = during the sale. No preposition needed – the noun plus 때 (ttae) does it all.
When the subject is someone honored, the verb usually takes -세요 (-seyo): 할머니는 좋아하세요 (halmeonineun joahaseyo) – grandma's verb gets the respect, not her name.
노트북 (noteubuk) looks like 'notebook' but means laptop – Konglish: 노트북을 샀어요 (noteubugeul sasseoyo) = bought a laptop. A paper notebook is 공책 (gongchaek).
켜지다 (kyeojida) = turn on by itself, the flip side of 켜다 (kyeoda = turn it on): 안 켜져요 (an kyeojyeoyo) = it won't come on, no matter who's pressing.
-지 마세요 = please don't: 보지 마세요 (boji maseyo) = don't look.
-(으)ㄹ 때 = when: 먹을 때 (meogeul ttae) = when eating.
없이 (eopsi) after a noun means without: 인터넷 없이 못 살아요 (inteonet eopsi mot sarayo) = can't live without the internet.
설날 (seollal) follows the lunar calendar – 음력 (eumnyeok) – so it lands in late January or February, never on January 1.
Koreans eat their age: 나이를 먹다 (naireul meokda) = get older, literally 'eat age'. 한 살 더 먹어요 (han sal deo meogeoyo) = eat one more year.
Koreans eat their age: 나이를 한 살 먹어요 (naireul han sal meogeoyo) is literally 'eat one year of age'. 먹다 (meokda = eat) is the normal way to say you get a year older.
